claims.text: High configurational entropy governs the structural stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles during high-temperature service.
High configurational entropy suppresses intermetallic-compound formation.
High configurational entropy promotes a random solid-solution structure.
The proposed intervention is heat treatment at 773–1173 K for catalytic operation and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use.
The hypothesis is intended to apply under high-temperature service with low noble-metal content.
Suppressing intermetallic formation and maintaining a random solid solution will improve nanoparticle structural stability.
Suppressing intermetallic formation and maintaining a random solid solution will improve nanoparticle chemical stability.
Stability will increase by 20% relative to traditional alloys.
Traditional alloys used as the baseline do not possess high configurational entropy.
The proposed mechanism applies over 773–1923 K at low noble-metal content.
The effect of configurational entropy on structural stability is not fully understood.
Structural stability may depend on the specific alloy composition.
Structural stability may depend on processing conditions.
A decrease in structural and chemical stability of more than 10% relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention includes thermoelectric testing from 473 K, whereas the stated boundary begins at 773 K, leaving 473–772 K simultaneously included in the experiment and outside the claimed applicability range.
